h2o.name: Water
h2o.description: The basis of life. Two lone pairs on oxygen bend the molecule, which makes water a polar solvent.

co2.name: Carbon dioxide
co2.description: A product of breathing and burning. Its two double bonds lie on one line, so the molecule is nonpolar.

ch4.name: Methane
ch4.description: The main component of natural gas. Four C–H bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron.

nh3.name: Ammonia
nh3.description: A pungent gas and raw material for fertilizers. The lone pair on nitrogen gives the molecule a pyramid shape.

ethanol.name: Ethanol
ethanol.description: A typical alcohol. Its –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

benzene.name: Benzene
benzene.description: An aromatic hydrocarbon. The electrons of its six carbon atoms are spread evenly around the ring.

nacl.name: Sodium chloride (table salt)
nacl.description: An ionic compound: not a molecule but a crystal lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Each ion is surrounded by 6 counter-ions.

h2so4.name: Sulfuric acid
h2so4.description: A strong diprotic acid and the key product of the chemical industry. Sulfur has an oxidation state of +6.

glucose.name: Glucose
glucose.description: A product of photosynthesis and the cell’s main energy source. In solution it exists mostly as a ring.

caffeine.name: Caffeine
caffeine.description: An alkaloid found in tea and coffee. A flat structure of two fused rings with four nitrogen atoms.

h2.name: Hydrogen
h2.description: The lightest gas. Two H atoms share one electron pair — a nonpolar covalent bond.

o2.name: Oxygen
o2.description: The gas needed for breathing and burning. The atoms are joined by a double bond; each O has two lone pairs.

n2.name: Nitrogen
n2.description: 78 % of air. The triple bond is very strong, so nitrogen is quite unreactive.

cl2.name: Chlorine
cl2.description: A yellow-green toxic gas. Two Cl atoms are joined by a single bond, each with three lone pairs.

o3.name: Ozone
o3.description: An allotrope of oxygen. Earth's ozone layer absorbs the Sun's UV light. A lone pair on the central atom bends the molecule.

hcl.name: Hydrogen chloride
hcl.description: Its solution in water is hydrochloric acid (also found in stomach juice). The H–Cl bond is polar: electron density shifts toward chlorine.

h2o2.name: Hydrogen peroxide
h2o2.description: Used to disinfect wounds. The O–O bond is weak, so it easily decomposes and releases oxygen.

co.name: Carbon monoxide
co.description: A colorless, odorless, very toxic gas that binds tightly to hemoglobin. One of its three bonds is a dative (donor–acceptor) bond.

so2.name: Sulfur dioxide
so2.description: A pungent gas that causes acid rain. A lone pair on sulfur bends the molecule.

hno3.name: Nitric acid
hno3.shape: Planar (nitrogen at the center of a triangle)
hno3.description: A strong acid and oxidizer used to make fertilizers and explosives.

h3po4.name: Phosphoric acid
h3po4.description: A moderately strong triprotic acid used in phosphate fertilizers and soft drinks.

ethane.name: Ethane
ethane.description: The second alkane, found in natural gas. Groups can rotate around the C–C bond.

propane.name: Propane
propane.description: Fuel in gas cylinders. Because of tetrahedral angles the carbon chain is a zigzag, not a straight line.

butane.name: Butane
butane.description: The gas in lighters. Same formula as isobutane (C₄H₁₀) but with an unbranched chain — structural isomerism.

isobutane.name: Isobutane (2-methylpropane)
isobutane.description: An isomer of butane: three CH₃ groups are attached to a central carbon. Used as a refrigerant.

ethylene.name: Ethylene (ethene)
ethylene.description: The simplest hydrocarbon with a double bond; the raw material for polyethylene, it speeds up fruit ripening.

acetylene.name: Acetylene (ethyne)
acetylene.description: A hydrocarbon with a triple bond. Its flame in oxygen reaches 3000 °C, so it is used for welding.

methanol.name: Methanol
methanol.description: The simplest alcohol; very toxic (a small dose can cause blindness). Used as a solvent and fuel.

dimethyl-ether.name: Dimethyl ether
dimethyl-ether.description: An isomer of ethanol (C₂H₆O) without an –OH group: oxygen sits between two carbons. That is why it is a gas at room temperature.

glycerol.name: Glycerol
glycerol.description: An alcohol with three –OH groups. A sweet, syrupy liquid used in cosmetics and medicines.

formaldehyde.name: Formaldehyde (methanal)
formaldehyde.description: The simplest aldehyde. Its water solution (formalin) preserves biological specimens; toxic.

acetic-acid.name: Acetic acid
acetic-acid.description: The basis of table vinegar. The –COOH (carboxyl) group makes it an acid.

acetone.name: Acetone (propanone)
acetone.description: The simplest ketone and a good solvent (nail-polish remover). An isomer of propanal: the C=O group is in the middle of the chain.

propanal.name: Propanal
propanal.description: An aldehyde: the C=O group is at the end of the chain. Same formula as acetone (C₃H₆O) — functional-group isomerism.

phenol.name: Phenol
phenol.description: A benzene ring with an –OH group. An antiseptic and a raw material for plastics; toxic.

sucrose.name: Sucrose
sucrose.description: Table sugar. A disaccharide made of glucose and fructose units; obtained from sugar beet and sugar cane.

urea.name: Urea
urea.description: A product of nitrogen metabolism. The first organic compound made in a lab (Wöhler, 1828); a nitrogen fertilizer.

glycine.name: Glycine
glycine.description: The simplest amino acid: it has both an –NH₂ (basic) and a –COOH (acidic) group. A building block of proteins.

alanine.name: Alanine
alanine.description: A protein amino acid. Its α-carbon carries four different groups, so it has two mirror-image forms (L and D) — chirality.

aspirin.name: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)
aspirin.description: A pain and fever reliever. The molecule has a benzene ring, a carboxyl group and an ester group.

vitamin-c.name: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)
vitamin-c.description: A vitamin needed for immunity and a strong reducing agent (antioxidant). Rich in citrus fruit and rose hips.

diamond.name: Diamond
diamond.description: An allotrope of carbon. Each atom is bonded to four neighbors (sp³), which makes diamond the hardest natural substance.

graphite.name: Graphite
graphite.description: An allotrope of carbon. Atoms in each layer form hexagons (sp²) and the layers are only weakly held together, so graphite is soft and conducts electricity.

ice.name: Ice
ice.description: Each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds (dashed lines) with four neighbors. The lattice has a lot of empty space, so ice is lighter than water and floats.

iron.name: Iron
iron.description: A metallic lattice: free electrons (an “electron sea”) move between positive ions, so metals conduct electricity and heat well.

copper.name: Copper
copper.description: One of the most tightly packed metal lattices. Copper is ductile and, after silver, the best electrical conductor — used for wires.

chat.title: Chemistry AI
chat.greeting: Hi! I’m your chemistry assistant. Pick one of the questions below and I’ll explain it step by step.

shape.q: Why is a water molecule bent?
shape.a:
1) The oxygen atom has 4 electron pairs around it: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs.
2) The four pairs point toward the corners of a tetrahedron.
3) Lone pairs repel the bonds more strongly, so the H–O–H angle is not 109.5° but about 104.5°.

Pick H₂O in the 3D viewer above and take a look.
shape.src: Source: Chemistry, grade 8, “Spatial structure of molecules”

ph.q: What is the pH of a 0.1 M HCl solution?
ph.a:
1) HCl is a strong acid and dissociates completely: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻.
2) So [H⁺] = 0.1 mol/L.
3) pH = −log[H⁺] = −log(0.1) = 1.

Check: the titration curve in the lab starts at exactly pH = 1.00 at 0 mL.

bonds.q: How do covalent and ionic bonds differ?
bonds.a:
Covalent bond: atoms share an electron pair (H₂O, CH₄, CO₂).
Ionic bond: an electron moves completely from one atom to another, and the oppositely charged ions attract each other (NaCl).

Remember: if the electronegativity difference is greater than about 1.7, the bond is mostly ionic.
bonds.src: Source: Chemistry, grade 8, “Types of chemical bonds”

categoryInfo.alkali: Group 1 metals (Li–Fr). Very reactive and soft enough to cut with a knife; react with water to form an alkali and hydrogen. 1 outer electron.
categoryInfo.alkaline-earth: Group 2 metals (Be–Ra). Less reactive and harder than alkali metals; their oxides form alkalis with water. 2 outer electrons.
categoryInfo.transition: Groups 3–12 metals (d-block). Strong, good conductors of heat and electricity, show several oxidation states, often form colored compounds.
categoryInfo.post-transition: Metals of the p-block (Al, Ga, In, Sn, Pb, Bi…). Soft with fairly low melting points; some form amphoteric oxides.
categoryInfo.metalloid: Elements between metals and nonmetals (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te). Mixed properties; many are semiconductors, the basis of electronics.
categoryInfo.nonmetal: Nonmetals (H, C, N, O, P, S, Se). Poor conductors with high electronegativity; the main elements of living things.
categoryInfo.halogen: Group 17 (F, Cl, Br, I, At, Ts). “Salt formers”: very reactive nonmetals that make salts with metals. 7 outer electrons.
categoryInfo.noble-gas: Group 18 (He–Og). Full outer shell (octet), so they hardly react; colorless, odorless gases.
categoryInfo.lanthanide: La–Lu (57–71), the 4f-block. Rare-earth metals used in magnets, lasers, screens and LEDs.
categoryInfo.actinide: Ac–Lr (89–103), the 5f-block. All radioactive; uranium and plutonium are nuclear fuels, elements after uranium are made artificially.

titration.goal: Find the concentration of hydrochloric acid (HCl) by titrating it with 0.1 M sodium hydroxide (NaOH).
titration.theory: When an acid reacts with a base, neutralisation takes place: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. The moment all the acid has reacted is the equivalence point. For a strong acid and a strong base the medium at this point is neutral (pH ≈ 7). Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic and neutral solutions and turns crimson in alkaline ones — stop at the first drop that gives a colour. At the equivalence point the amounts are equal: c(HCl)·V(HCl) = c(NaOH)·V(NaOH).

mixture-separation.goal: Recover pure sand and salt from a mixture of sand, table salt and water, and calculate the yield of salt.
mixture-separation.theory: Mixtures are separated using differences in the properties of their components. Table salt (NaCl) dissolves well in water, sand does not. So first we dissolve the mixture in water, then filter it through filter paper: the insoluble sand stays on the filter while the salt solution (filtrate) passes through. Evaporating the filtrate in a porcelain dish removes the water and leaves salt crystals. The wet sand on the filter is dried. Yield: η = m(obtained) / m(initial) · 100%.

atom-builder.goal: Choose the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons to build atom and ion models; identify the element, mass number and charge.
atom-builder.theory: An atom consists of a positively charged nucleus with electrons moving around it. The nucleus contains protons (charge +1) and neutrons (charge 0). The element is determined by the number of protons — it equals the atomic number (Z). Mass number: A = protons + neutrons. An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so it is neutral. An atom that loses an electron becomes a positive ion (cation, e.g. Na⁺); one that gains an electron becomes a negative ion (anion, e.g. Cl⁻). Electrons fill shells: up to 2 in the 1st, up to 8 in the 2nd and up to 8 in the 3rd (Z ≤ 20).

indicator-lab.goal: Use indicator colours to find the medium (acidic, neutral, alkaline) of six unknown solutions.
indicator-lab.theory: An indicator is a substance that changes colour depending on the medium of a solution. The medium is described by pH: pH < 7 — acidic, pH = 7 — neutral, pH > 7 — alkaline. Each indicator changes colour in its own pH range: litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali; phenolphthalein turns crimson only in alkaline solutions (pH > 8.2); methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in neutral and alkaline solutions. A universal indicator shows a full colour scale, so it lets you estimate the pH.

reaction-rate.goal: Investigate how temperature and concentration affect the rate of the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid.
reaction-rate.theory: Reaction: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂↑. A gas syringe measures the volume of hydrogen released. The reaction rate is the amount of product formed per unit time. When the temperature rises, particles move faster and collide more often — by van 't Hoff's rule the rate grows γ times for every 10 °C. Raising the concentration also makes collisions more frequent. There is little magnesium (0.05 g) and it is the limiting reagent, so the final volume is the same in every case. The half-time t½ is the time for half of the volume to form: the higher the rate, the smaller t½.

precipitation.goal: Add reagents to salt solutions, find out when a precipitate forms and write net ionic equations for the exchange reactions.
precipitation.theory: When electrolyte solutions are mixed, their ions swap partners. An exchange reaction goes to completion if one of the products is a precipitate (an insoluble substance), a gas or water. balance-equations.goal: Balance simple reaction equations with coefficients and show that the number of atoms is conserved.
balance-equations.theory: In a chemical reaction atoms are neither destroyed nor created — they only regroup. So each element must have the same number of atoms on the left and on the right of an equation (the law of conservation of mass, M. Lomonosov, A. Lavoisier). To balance an equation, put coefficients in front of the substances: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. A coefficient shows the number of molecules, while a subscript shows what a molecule is made of. Never change subscripts: writing H₂O₂ instead of H₂O gives a different substance. Coefficients must be the smallest whole numbers.

mass-fraction.goal: Calculate the mass fraction of a solute and prepare three solutions of given concentration.
mass-fraction.theory: The mass fraction of a solute is the ratio of its mass to the total mass of the solution: w = m(solute) / m(solution) · 100 %. The mass of the solution is the mass of the solute plus the mass of water. Water has a density of 1 g/mL, so 1 mL of water = 1 g. For example, 50 g of a 10 % solution needs 5 g of salt and 45 g of water. Adding water lowers w, evaporating raises it.

equilibrium.goal: Test Le Chatelier’s principle: find which way an equilibrium shifts when temperature, pressure and concentration change.
equilibrium.theory: When the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal, the system is at chemical equilibrium. Le Chatelier’s principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts so as to reduce the disturbance. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, and adding a substance favours the reaction that uses it up. A catalyst does not shift an equilibrium. We study N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ (ΔH > 0; NO₂ is a brown gas) and Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN²⁺ (blood red).

redox.goal: Observe electron transfer in reactions of metals with salts and an acid, and identify the oxidising and reducing agents.
redox.theory: In redox reactions the oxidation states of particles change because electrons move from one particle to another. The particle that gives away electrons is the reducing agent, and it is itself oxidised: Zn⁰ − 2e⁻ → Zn²⁺. The particle that accepts electrons is the oxidising agent, and it is reduced: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu⁰. The numbers of electrons lost and gained must be equal (electron balance). A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its salt.

dissociation.goal: Compare the electrical conductivity of solutions and identify strong electrolytes, weak electrolytes and non-electrolytes.
dissociation.theory: Electrolytes are substances that break up into ions in solution or when molten, so they conduct electricity. Strong electrolytes (most salts, HCl, NaOH) dissociate almost completely: NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻. In weak electrolytes (CH₃COOH, NH₃·H₂O) only a small fraction of molecules break up — the degree of dissociation α is small. Non-electrolytes (sugar, alcohol) form no ions when they dissolve and do not conduct. For a weak electrolyte α is found from Ostwald’s law: α ≈ √(K / c).

galvanic-cell.goal: Build galvanic cells from different metals, measure their EMF and identify the anode and the cathode.
galvanic-cell.theory: In a galvanic cell the energy of a chemical reaction becomes electrical energy. Two metals are dipped into solutions of their own salts and joined by a salt bridge. The more reactive metal (lower electrode potential) is the anode: it is oxidised and dissolves (Zn − 2e⁻ → Zn²⁺). The other metal is the cathode: ions from the solution are reduced on it (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). Electrons flow through the external circuit from the anode to the cathode. Standard EMF = E°(cathode) − E°(anode). E°: Mg −2.37; Zn −0.76; Fe −0.44; Cu +0.34; Ag +0.80 V.

organic-properties.goal: Use qualitative tests to identify the class (functional group) of six organic substances.
organic-properties.theory: The properties of organic substances depend on their functional groups, so each class has its own qualitative test. Alkenes with a double bond decolourise bromine water. Polyhydric alcohols (glycerol, glucose) give a deep blue solution with freshly made Cu(OH)₂. The aldehyde group (–CHO) gives the silver mirror test. Carboxylic acids (–COOH) release CO₂ with baking soda. Hydrocarbons do not dissolve in water and form a separate layer. Glucose is both a polyhydric alcohol and an aldehyde.

organic-builder.goal: Build three pairs of isomers in the molecule builder and show that substances with the same composition can differ in structure and class.
organic-builder.theory: Isomers are substances with the same molecular formula but a different structure (the order in which the atoms are joined). For example, C₄H₁₀ is both butane (a chain) and isobutane (branched). Isomers can even belong to different classes: C₂H₆O is ethanol (an alcohol, –OH) and dimethyl ether (an ether, C–O–C); C₃H₆O is propanal (an aldehyde, –CHO) and acetone (a ketone, C=O in the middle of the chain). In a structural formula carbon has a valency of 4, oxygen 2 and hydrogen 1.

Legal.note: These are the platform's short, plain-language rules. Before using it at school, agree them with the school administration.

collect.title: What data we collect
collect.text: When you create an account: name, email, role (student or teacher), grade and school (optional). When you use the platform: test, experiment and olympiad results, XP, questions to the AI tutor, and classes and assignments created by teachers.

purpose.title: What it is used for
purpose.text: Data is used only for learning: saving results, showing a student's progress to their teacher and finding weak topics. There are no ads, and data is not sold or shared with other organisations.

camera.title: Camera
camera.text: During QR scanning, hand gestures and AR, camera frames are processed only on your device. They are never sent to the server or stored.

ai.title: AI tutor
ai.text: Only the text of your question is sent to the AI tutor (Google Gemini). Your name and email are never sent to the AI. Do not write personal details about yourself in the chat.

storage.title: Where it is stored
storage.text: Data is stored in a Supabase database over a secure connection with strict access rules (RLS). The site runs on Vercel. A student's results are visible only to the student and their class teacher.

minors.title: Minors
minors.text: Students under 16 use the platform with the consent of a parent (legal guardian) or the school. When it is used in class, the teacher and school arrange the consent.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.text: Under the Law of Kazakhstan on Personal Data and its Protection you may view, correct and delete your data. The “Delete account” button on the profile page permanently deletes the account and all results.

contact.title: Contact
contact.text: Ask your teacher or the school administration about your data.

purpose.title: Purpose
purpose.text: CHEMVERSE AI is an educational platform for learning chemistry. It complements the teacher's lessons but does not replace the textbook or the teacher.

ai.title: AI answers
ai.text: The AI tutor and AI-generated plans can make mistakes. Check important information against the textbook or with your teacher. Lesson plans generated by AI are reviewed and approved by the teacher.

labs.title: Virtual lab
labs.text: Virtual experiment results are a learning model, not real measurements. Do real experiments only with a teacher and following safety rules.

accounts.title: Account
accounts.text: Never share your password, and sign out on shared computers. Demo accounts are shared: other people see changes made in them.

conduct.title: Conduct
conduct.text: Use the platform only for learning. Do not insult others, deliberately break the system or use the AI for things unrelated to chemistry.

changes.title: Changes
changes.text: These rules may be updated. After important changes, the date on this page changes.

About.title: CHEMVERSE AI: chemistry you can see and touch
About.lead: A chemistry platform that brings teachers and students together: 3D and AR molecules, a virtual lab, an AI tutor in Kazakh, UNT and olympiad preparation and live class quizzes.

problem.title: The problem
problem.text: Chemistry is abstract: students only see molecules as textbook drawings. Many schools lack lab equipment and reagents, UNT preparation materials are scattered, and teachers have little time to prepare lessons.

solution.title: The solution
solution.text: Students rotate molecules in 3D, place them on the desk through the phone camera and control them with hand gestures. In the virtual lab they safely run grade 7–10 experiments that the server grades. The AI tutor answers in Kazakh, step by step, grounded in textbook summaries.

teacher.title: For teachers
teacher.text: Classes and assignments, students' test and lab results, live class quizzes (Kahoot-style), AI-assisted lesson plans and QR codes for textbooks and slides. Teachers review and approve every AI-generated plan.

safety.title: Safety
safety.text: Camera frames are processed only on the device. Test answers are checked on the server and correct answers are never sent in advance. Students' names are never sent to the AI. A student's data is visible only to the student and their teacher.

tech.title: Technology
tech.text: Next.js, Supabase (RLS access rules), Google Gemini with a knowledge base built from textbook summaries (RAG), 3Dmol.js and Three.js, MediaPipe (hand gestures) and AR. The site installs on phones as an app (PWA), and there is an Android APK. The interface is in Kazakh, Russian and English.
